Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture

Abhijeet Mulgund ††thanks: This work was supported by NSF under awards 2240532 and 2217023. Affiliation: University of Illinois Chicago Email: mulgund2@uic.edu
Abstract

Let RR be an m×mm\times m correlation matrix satisfying R−𝟏𝟏𝖳/m⪰0R-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}/m\succeq 0, let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R), and let Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} be independent standard Gaussian random variables. We prove

maxiXi≤stmaxiZi,\max_{i}X_{i}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\max_{i}Z_{i},

with equality in distribution if and only if R=ImR=I_{m}. We use this comparison to resolve the Weak Simplex Conjecture: among d+1d+1 equiprobable equal-energy signals in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} transmitted over an additive white Gaussian noise channel, the regular simplex is the unique maximizer of the average probability of correct maximum-likelihood decoding at every positive signal-to-noise ratio. The same comparison proves the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture and gives the exact finite-energy performance of deterministic no-feedback AWGN codes with equiprobable messages, no restriction on the number of channel uses, and a maximal per-codeword energy constraint.

The proof uses a Gaussian product inequality for log-concave functions whose first moments with respect to standard Gaussian measure vanish. A variational argument chooses one exponential tilt and one truncation endpoint in each coordinate so that this product inequality applies and a Gaussian change of measure returns all coordinates to the prescribed common threshold. A strict form of the product inequality also shows that, unless R=ImR=I_{m}, ℙ{X≤c𝟏}>Φ(c)m\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}>\Phi(c)^{m} for every finite cc, and hence gives the distributional equality statement. A Lean formalization is available at https://github.com/abhmul/weak-simplex-conjecture-lean.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 60E15; Secondary 52A40, 94A24, 94B70.

Keywords. Gaussian maxima, stochastic domination, Gaussian inequalities, Weak Simplex Conjecture, simplex mean width, AWGN codes.

1 Introduction

The Weak Simplex Conjecture traces back to an observation of Shannon reported by Rice in 1950 [30]; the name was later coined by Massey in 1988 [21]. It asks how to place m=d+1m=d+1 equiprobable signals of equal energy in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} when the channel adds isotropic Gaussian noise and the receiver uses maximum-likelihood decoding. The conjecture asserts that the vertices of a regular simplex maximize the average probability of correct decoding at every positive signal-to-noise ratio. If the unit signal vectors are x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}, if G=(⟨xi,xj⟩)i,jG=(\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle)_{i,j} is their Gram matrix, and if λ>0\lambda>0 is the signal-to-noise ratio, then the correct decoding probability satisfies

Pc​(x1,…,xm,λ)=e−λ2/2m​𝔼​exp⁡{λ​max1≤i≤m​ξi},ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G).P_{\mathrm{c}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m};\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\xi_{i}\right\},\qquad\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G). (1)

We refer to ξ\xi as the score vector for the code with Gram matrix GG, since its coordinates are the random parts of the maximum-likelihood scores. Thus the conjecture is equivalent to an extremal problem for the moment-generating function of a Gaussian maximum. The difficulty lies in the failure of the usual entrywise covariance comparisons, such as Slepian’s inequality [34], to settle the problem: an arbitrary competing Gram matrix need not be entrywise comparable with the regular-simplex Gram matrix.

Our main theorem is a stochastic comparison. Write J=𝟏𝟏𝖳J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}. If RR is a correlation matrix satisfying

R−1m​J⪰0,R-\frac{1}{m}J\succeq 0, (2)

then, for X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R) and independent standard Gaussian random variables Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m},

ℙ{maxiXi≤c}≥Φ(c)m=ℙ{maxiZi≤c}(c∈ℝ).\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\max_{i}X_{i}\leq c\right\}\geq\Phi(c)^{m}=\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\max_{i}Z_{i}\leq c\right\}\qquad(c\in\mathbb{R}). (3)

Equivalently, maxiXi≤stmaxiZi\max_{i}X_{i}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\max_{i}Z_{i}. Furthermore, the two maxima have the same distribution if and only if R=ImR=I_{m}. The common threshold in (3) is essential: the analogous comparison for arbitrary threshold vectors is false; see Remark 2.2. The direct proof in Appendix B gives the stronger conclusion that the inequality is strict at every finite cc when R≠ImR\neq I_{m}.

The coding problem is connected to (3) by adding the same independent Gaussian random variable to every score and then rescaling. On covariance matrices, this operation is

R=m−1m​G+1m​J.R=\frac{m-1}{m}G+\frac{1}{m}J. (4)

It sends the regular-simplex Gram matrix mm−1​(Im−J/m)\frac{m}{m-1}(I_{m}-J/m) to ImI_{m}. If λ=(m−1)/m​μ\lambda=\sqrt{(m-1)/m}\,\mu, then the corresponding Gaussian maxima satisfy

e−μ2/2𝔼eμ​maxi​Xi=e−λ2/2𝔼eλ​maxi​ξi.e^{-\mu^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\max_{i}X_{i}}=e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}. (5)

Combining (3)–(5) with (1) proves the Weak Simplex Conjecture. The equality statement also shows that the regular simplex is the unique maximizer, up to orthogonal transformation and relabeling, at every λ>0\lambda>0. This also yields the exact optimal decoding probability in the deterministic no-feedback finite-energy additive white-Gaussian noise (AWGN) model of Corollary 2.8.

Another consequence is the following bound on expected maxima of Gaussian random variables. Since the added Gaussian random variable has mean zero,

𝔼​maxi​ξi=mm−1​𝔼​maxi​Xi.\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}\,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}X_{i}. (6)

Applying (3) to the identity function proves [19, Conjecture 1.4], which is equivalent to the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture [19, Conjecture 1.1]. Thus the regular simplex uniquely maximizes mean width among convex hulls of mm points in the unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} whenever d≥m−1d\geq m-1.

1.1 Proof idea

The first ingredient is a Gaussian product inequality. Let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R), where RR is any correlation matrix. If bounded log-concave functions fi:ℝ→[0,∞)f_{i}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty) satisfy

∫ℝz​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0,\int_{\mathbb{R}}zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0, (7)

then

𝔼​∏ifi​(Xi)≥∏i∫fi​d​γ1.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i}f_{i}(X_{i})\geq\prod_{i}\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}.

After division by its Gaussian integral, each factor in (7) defines a probability measure of mean zero. The product inequality is a specialization of the centered Gaussian forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb theorem of Milman, Nakamura, and Tsuji [22]; we record the specialization and give a direct proof in Appendix B.

The indicator of (−∞,c](-\infty,c] has the correct product but not the required first moment. We repair this by multiplying by an exponential and allowing the endpoint to move. Set

r⁡(s)=φ⁡(s)Φ⁡(s),H⁡(s)=s+r⁡(s).r(s)=\frac{\varphi(s)}{\Phi(s)},\qquad H(s)=s+r(s). (8)

Then

fs(z)=er⁡(s)​z𝟏(−∞,H(s)](z)f_{s}(z)=e^{r(s)z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,H(s)]}(z) (9)

satisfies ∫z​fs​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0\int zf_{s}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0. Applying this exponential tilt shifts the mean of XX. If one parameter sis_{i} is chosen for each coordinate and ai=r⁡(si)a_{i}=r(s_{i}), a Gaussian change of measure returns to the event in (3) precisely when

s+a−R​a=c​𝟏.s+a-Ra=c\mathbf{1}. (10)

The logarithm of the Gaussian mass of (9), viewed as a function of its endpoint H⁡(s)H(s), has derivative r⁡(s)r(s). This identity turns the coupled equations in (10) into the stationarity equations of a strictly concave finite-dimensional functional. Its maximizer also gives

∑i=1mlog⁡Φ⁡(si)+12​a𝖳​(Im−R)​a≥m​log⁡Φ⁡(c),\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Phi(s_{i})+\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a\geq m\log\Phi(c), (11)

which is exactly the remaining estimate needed after the product inequality and the Gaussian change of measure are combined.

The same product argument also gives the equality statement. For the truncated exponential factors above, the product inequality is strict whenever R≠ImR\neq I_{m}. It follows that the common-threshold comparison is strict at every finite cc, so the maximum laws can agree only when R=ImR=I_{m}. For completeness, Appendix C gives a different proof that applies to arbitrary centered Gaussian vectors, without the unit-variance or semidefinite hypotheses of the main theorem.

1.2 Relation to prior work

The Weak Simplex Conjecture originates in Shannon’s work on communication over Gaussian channels [30, 32]. Balakrishnan proved several partial results [2, 3, 4]. Landau and Slepian gave an argument valid in dimension three [18]; Tanner explained why it does not extend to all dimensions [39, 40]. Later formulations appear in Farber’s thesis, Cover’s problem list, and Massey’s Shannon Lecture [11, 9, 21]. The equal-codeword-energy Weak Simplex Conjecture is distinct from the average-energy Strong Simplex Conjecture, which Steiner disproved [35].

The formulations in terms of Gaussian maxima and mean width were developed in [5, 16, 19]. Sun, Hu, and Lan proved the four-variable Gaussian maximum case and the three-dimensional mean-width case [37]. Guédon and Souli extend a Chevet comparison inequality to a broader class of smooth functions and prove their comparison for a block-structured family of Gaussian vectors [14]. Their Conjecture 1.6 records the Gaussian expected-maximum formulation of the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture resolved here.

The product inequality used in the proof is related to the Šidák–Khatri inequality and the Gaussian correlation theorem [17, 33, 15, 31, 1]. Its present form follows from the forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb framework of Liu, Courtade, Cuff, and Verdú [20], together with the centered Gaussian results of Milman, Nakamura, and Tsuji [23, 24, 25, 22]. Nakamura and Tsuji’s equality theorem for two centered convex sets also implies the equality case for finite symmetric rectangles. The direct proof in Appendix B is shorter for the product form needed here.

Independent work on strictness and equality.

After version 1 of this paper was posted, the present author and Su et al. independently obtained the pointwise strictness and equality cases [36]. A complete formal proof in the companion Lean repository was committed on 19 July 202611 1 See See commit d7b8419.; the branch was merged into the public main branch on 14 August 2026, and the result was incorporated into the revision of this manuscript dated 20 August 2026. Su et al. obtain the same strict common-threshold conclusion by strengthening the first normalized self-convolution step: they first isolate a strict bivariate rectangle gap and then use Royen’s Gaussian correlation theorem to group the remaining coordinate slabs. The direct proof here instead proves the full strict rectangle inequality by conditioning and induction. Thus the two pointwise strictness proofs share the self-convolution framework of the direct centered-product proof in Appendix B, but establish the decisive strict rectangle input differently. We regard them as independent parallel resolutions; the original question is retained as the resolved Problem 8.1.

Prior announced proofs.

Two earlier preprints announce proofs: Goldsmith for the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture and Pastore for the Weak Simplex Conjecture [12, 26]. Our proof is independent of both. In Appendix D we give a version-specific account of unresolved steps in the respective submissions arXiv:2112.03393v2 and arXiv:2306.13478v2 that prevent us from using their announced conclusions. That discussion concerns only those posted versions and does not rule out repairs or later arguments.

1.3 Organization

Sections 2 and 3 state the main consequences and reduce the coding problem to the covariance comparison. The proof then proceeds in three stages: Section 4 supplies the Gaussian product inequality, Section 5 constructs compatible centered factors, and Section 6 combines them. Section 7 then returns to the coding and geometric applications. The appendices contain the one-dimensional calculations, a direct proof and strict form of the product inequality, a proof that a centered Gaussian vector whose maximum has the same law as the maximum of independent standard Gaussians must have covariance ImI_{m}, a version-specific discussion of two prior proof claims, and the details needed to apply the Weak Simplex Conjecture to the AWGN sequence model of [27].

2 Main results

The central comparison is most naturally stated for the transformed covariance RR. We state it first and then record the consequences obtained after returning to the original score covariance GG.

Throughout, m≥2m\geq 2, 𝟏=(1,…,1)𝖳∈ℝm\mathbf{1}=(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and J=𝟏𝟏𝖳J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}. We write γk\gamma_{k} for standard Gaussian measure on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}, and φ\varphi and Φ\Phi for the standard Gaussian density and distribution function, respectively. All logarithms are natural, and vector inequalities such as x≤yx\leq y are coordinatewise. A correlation matrix is a positive-semidefinite matrix with unit diagonal and may be singular. For real random variables UU and VV, we write U≤stVU\leq_{\mathrm{st}}V when ℙ{U>t}≤ℙ{V>t}\mathbb{P}\{U>t\}\leq\mathbb{P}\{V>t\} for every t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

Let

𝖬X=max1≤i≤m⁡Xi,𝖬Z=max1≤i≤m⁡Zi,\mathsf{M}_{X}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}X_{i},\qquad\mathsf{M}_{Z}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}Z_{i},

where Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} are independent standard Gaussian random variables.

Theorem 2.1.

Let RR be an m×mm\times m correlation matrix satisfying

R−1m​J⪰0,R-\frac{1}{m}J\succeq 0,

and let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R). Then

𝖬X≤st𝖬Z.\mathsf{M}_{X}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\mathsf{M}_{Z}. (12)

Equivalently,

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}≥Φ(c)mfor every c∈ℝ.\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}\geq\Phi(c)^{m}\qquad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}. (13)

Moreover,

𝖬X=d𝖬Z⟺R=Im.\mathsf{M}_{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\mathsf{M}_{Z}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad R=I_{m}. (14)

The event in (13) is the lower orthant (−∞,c]m(-\infty,c]^{m} with the same threshold cc in every coordinate. This restriction cannot be removed.

Remark 2.2.

Let

R=(1−1/31/3−1/311/31/31/31).R=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1/3&1/3\\ -1/3&1&1/3\\ 1/3&1/3&1\end{pmatrix}.

Then R−J/3⪰0R-J/3\succeq 0; indeed it is 2/32/3 times the Gram matrix of e1,−e1,e2e_{1},-e_{1},e_{2}. If X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R), the correlation of X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} is −1/3-1/3, so Sheppard’s Lemma gives

ℙ⁡{X1≤0,X2≤0}=14−12​π​arcsin⁡(13)<14.\mathbb{P}\{X_{1}\leq 0,X_{2}\leq 0\}=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)<\frac{1}{4}.

As L→∞L\to\infty, ℙ⁡{X1≤0,X2≤0,X3≤L}\mathbb{P}\{X_{1}\leq 0,X_{2}\leq 0,X_{3}\leq L\} tends to the left-hand side, whereas Φ​(0)2​Φ​(L)\Phi(0)^{2}\Phi(L) tends to 1/41/4. Hence, for all sufficiently large finite LL,

ℙ{X≤(0,0,L)𝖳}<Φ(0)2Φ(L).\mathbb{P}\{X\leq(0,0,L)^{\mathsf{T}}\}<\Phi(0)^{2}\Phi(L).

Thus the comparison in Theorem 2.1 can only apply to a common-threshold statement; an arbitrary lower-orthant comparison does not hold in general.

Remark 2.3.

The applications below require only the equality-in-distribution statement in (14). Theorem B.6 proves the stronger pointwise statement

R≠Im⟹ℙ{X≤c𝟏}>Φ(c)mfor every finite c.R\neq I_{m}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}>\Phi(c)^{m}\quad\text{for every finite }c.

Thus equality at even one finite threshold cc forces R=ImR=I_{m}. The same pointwise refinement was obtained independently by Su et al. [36, Theorem 1]. An independent argument in Appendix C proves the equality-in-distribution statement for an arbitrary centered Gaussian vector.

2.1 Consequences for Gaussian maxima and simplex codes

The advantage of the distributional comparison is that it controls every nondecreasing function of the maximum, rather than one moment-generating function at a time. The equality statement also makes these comparisons strict for strictly increasing integrable functions.

Corollary 2.4.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1, every nonnegative, nondecreasing Borel function ψ\psi satisfies

𝔼​ψ​(𝖬X)≤𝔼​ψ​(𝖬Z),\mathbb{E}\psi(\mathsf{M}_{X})\leq\mathbb{E}\psi(\mathsf{M}_{Z}),

including when one or both expectations are infinite. If R≠ImR\neq I_{m}, ψ:ℝ→ℝ\psi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is strictly increasing, and ψ⁡(𝖬X)\psi(\mathsf{M}_{X}) and ψ⁡(𝖬Z)\psi(\mathsf{M}_{Z}) are integrable, then

𝔼​ψ​(𝖬X)<𝔼​ψ​(𝖬Z).\mathbb{E}\psi(\mathsf{M}_{X})<\mathbb{E}\psi(\mathsf{M}_{Z}).

In particular, for every λ>0\lambda>0,

𝔼eλ​𝖬X<𝔼eλ​𝖬Z,𝔼𝖬X<𝔼𝖬Z(R≠Im).\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\mathsf{M}_{X}}<\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\mathsf{M}_{Z}},\qquad\mathbb{E}\mathsf{M}_{X}<\mathbb{E}\mathsf{M}_{Z}\qquad(R\neq I_{m}).

We now return from the transformed covariance RR to the score covariance GG. Set

G△=mm−1​(Im−1m​J).G_{\triangle}=\frac{m}{m-1}\left(I_{m}-\frac{1}{m}J\right). (15)

This is the Gram matrix of the vertices of a regular (m−1)(m-1)-simplex inscribed in the unit sphere. Conversely, any unit-vector configuration with this Gram matrix is a regular simplex, up to an orthogonal transformation and relabeling. Under the covariance transformation in (4), G△G_{\triangle} is sent to ImI_{m}. Thus Theorem 2.1 compares every score covariance with the regular-simplex covariance.

Corollary 2.5.

Let GG be any m×mm\times m correlation matrix, let ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G), and let ξ△∼𝒩⁡(0,G△)\xi^{\triangle}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\triangle}). Then

𝔼​exp​{λ​maxi​ξi}≤𝔼​exp​{λ​maxi​ξi△}(λ>0).\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}\right\}\leq\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}\right\}\qquad(\lambda>0). (16)

If G≠G△G\neq G_{\triangle}, then (16) is strict for every λ>0\lambda>0. Equivalently, equality for any one λ>0\lambda>0 holds if and only if G=G△G=G_{\triangle}.

Combining the preceding MGF comparison with the maximum-likelihood identity in Section 3 gives the coding theorem in its classical form.

Corollary 2.6 (Weak Simplex Conjecture).

Let m=d+1m=d+1, let x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} be unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let the message II be uniform on {1,…,m}\{1,\ldots,m\}. Under the channel

Y=λ​xI+Z,Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),λ>0,Y=\lambda x_{I}+Z,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),\quad\lambda>0,

the average probability of correct maximum-likelihood decoding is no larger than for a regular simplex. For every fixed λ>0\lambda>0, equality holds if and only if the xix_{i} form a regular simplex. Thus the regular simplex is the unique maximizer up to rotation and relabeling.

The single-parameter MGF rigidity in Corollary 2.5 and the strict coding equality case in Corollary 2.6 were obtained independently by Su et al. [36, Theorems 2 and 3(a)].

The comparison in Corollary 2.5 applies to Gram matrices of mm unit vectors in any Euclidean space. When the ambient dimension is at least m−1m-1, the regular simplex is attainable. In lower dimension it remains a universal upper bound, but we do not identify the best Gram matrix under a rank constraint.

The expected-maximum comparison extends from correlation matrices to covariance matrices whose marginal variances are at most one. This is the form that directly contains the geometric problem.

Corollary 2.7 (Gaussian maxima and the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture).

Let SS be an m×mm\times m positive-semidefinite matrix with Si​i≤1S_{ii}\leq 1, and let Y∼𝒩⁡(0,S)Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,S). Then

𝔼​maxi​Yi≤𝔼​maxi​ξi△=mm−1​𝔼​maxi​Zi,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}Y_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}\,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}Z_{i}, (17)

where ξ△∼𝒩⁡(0,G△)\xi^{\triangle}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\triangle}). Equality holds if and only if S=G△S=G_{\triangle}.

Consequently, among convex hulls of mm points contained in the Euclidean unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, for every d≥m−1d\geq m-1, the regular (m−1)(m-1)-simplex uniquely maximizes mean width, up to rotation and relabeling.

The equality case in Corollary 2.7 was obtained independently by Su et al. [36, Corollary 4].

2.2 Finite-energy AWGN consequence

The simplex theorem also determines the optimal probability of error for the AWGN channel when the number of channel uses is unrestricted. Following [27, Definition 1], fix E≥0E\geq 0 and N0>0N_{0}>0 and consider the AWGN sequence model Y=X+ZY=X+Z over ℝ∞\mathbb{R}^{\infty}, with independent noise coordinates of variance N0/2N_{0}/2. An (E,M,ϵ)(E,M,\epsilon) code consists of MM equiprobable codewords ci∈ℓ2c_{i}\in\ell_{2} satisfying ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E, together with a decoder whose average error probability is at most ϵ\epsilon.

This model imposes no constraint on the number of channel uses or nonzero codeword coordinates. For each fixed codebook, equal-prior maximum-likelihood decoding is Bayes-optimal. Let Pc∗​(E,M)P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M) be the largest average correct-decoding probability over admissible encoders and decoders, and let M∗​(E,ϵ)M^{*}(E,\epsilon) be the largest number of messages that can be communicated with error at most ϵ\epsilon. Let E∗​(M,ϵ)E^{*}(M,\epsilon) be the minimum energy needed to communicate MM messages with error at most ϵ\epsilon. For M≥2M\geq 2, define

pM​(a)=𝔼​Φ​(W+a)M−1,W∼𝒩⁡(0,1).p_{M}(a)=\mathbb{E}\Phi(W+a)^{M-1},\qquad W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). (18)
Corollary 2.8.

In the preceding model, the optimal correct-decoding probability is

Pc∗​(E,M)=pM​(2​E​M(M−1)​N0),M≥2.P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M)=p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right),\qquad M\geq 2. (19)

Hence, for 0≤ϵ<10\leq\epsilon<1,

M∗​(E,ϵ)=max⁡({1}∪{M≥2:pM​(2​E​M(M−1)​N0)≥1−ϵ}).M^{*}(E,\epsilon)=\max\!\left(\{1\}\cup\left\{M\geq 2:p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right)\geq 1-\epsilon\right\}\right). (20)

If 0<ϵ<1−1/M0<\epsilon<1-1/M, there is a unique aM,ϵ>0a_{M,\epsilon}>0 satisfying pM​(aM,ϵ)=1−ϵp_{M}(a_{M,\epsilon})=1-\epsilon, and the minimum energy for MM messages at error ϵ\epsilon is

E∗​(M,ϵ)=N02​M−1M​aM,ϵ2.E^{*}(M,\epsilon)=\frac{N_{0}}{2}\frac{M-1}{M}a_{M,\epsilon}^{2}. (21)

For ϵ≥1−1/M\epsilon\geq 1-1/M, E∗​(M,ϵ)E^{*}(M,\epsilon) is zero, whereas for ϵ=0\epsilon=0 it is infinite.

Equality in the finite-energy bound.

For E>0E>0, Su et al. independently characterize all optimizers [36, Theorem 3(b)]: an admissible MM-message codebook attains (19) if and only if

∑i=1Mci=0,∥ci∥2=E,⟨ci,cj⟩=−EM−1(i≠j).\sum_{i=1}^{M}c_{i}=0,\qquad\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}=E,\qquad\langle c_{i},c_{j}\rangle=-\frac{E}{M-1}\quad(i\neq j).

Thus the optimizer is a centered regular simplex of circumradius E\sqrt{E}, up to isometry of its span and relabeling, and every optimal codeword exhausts the energy allowance. This equality characterization supplements the optimal-value formula above.

Remark 2.9 (Relation to pulse-position modulation).

Orthogonal pulse-position modulation (PPM) has codewords E​e1,…,E​eM\sqrt{E}e_{1},\ldots,\sqrt{E}e_{M}. After subtracting its common center, it becomes a regular simplex of squared radius E⁡(M−1)/ME(M-1)/M. Its correct-decoding probability is therefore

pM​(2​EN0).p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E}{N_{0}}}\right).

Equivalently, the full-energy simplex at energy EE has the same performance as orthogonal PPM at energy E​M/(M−1)EM/(M-1). Corollary 2.6 then explains why the orthogonal PPM construction in [27] nearly obtains E∗​(M,ϵ)E^{*}(M,\epsilon).

We now turn to the proof of Theorem 2.1, beginning with the passage from the Gram matrix to the transformed covariance R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m.

3 From Gaussian classification to a covariance comparison

We now establish the reduction transforming the original coding problem with signal vectors x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} to Theorem 2.1.

3.1 The maximum-likelihood integral

Let x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} be unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Conditional on message ii, the channel output YY has density

pi(y)=(2π)−d/2exp(−12∥y−λxi∥2).p_{i}(y)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|y-\lambda x_{i}\|^{2}\right).

Since ‖xi‖=1\|x_{i}\|=1,

pi(y)=(2π)−d/2e−∥y∥2/2−λ2/2eλ​⟨y,xi⟩.p_{i}(y)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|y\|^{2}/2-\lambda^{2}/2}e^{\lambda\langle y,x_{i}\rangle}.

Only the last factor depends on ii, so maximum-likelihood decoding selects an index maximizing ⟨y,xi⟩\langle y,x_{i}\rangle. Let Di⊆ℝdD_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be the decision region assigned to message ii, using any measurable rule on ties. The regions form a partition, and pi​(y)=maxj⁡pj​(y)p_{i}(y)=\max_{j}p_{j}(y) on DiD_{i}. Hence

Pc​(x1,…,xm,λ)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{c}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m};\lambda) =1m​∑i=1m∫Dipi​(y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{D_{i}}p_{i}(y)\,dy
=e−λ2/2m​∫ℝdeλ​maxi​⟨y,xi⟩​d​γd​(y).\displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\langle y,x_{i}\rangle}\,d\gamma_{d}(y).

If Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and ξi=⟨Z,xi⟩\xi_{i}=\langle Z,x_{i}\rangle, then ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G) for G=(⟨xi,xj⟩)G=(\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle), and we get

Pc​(x1,…,xm,λ)=e−λ2/2m​𝔼​exp⁡{λ​maxi​ξi}.P_{\mathrm{c}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m};\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}\right\}. (22)

This also shows directly that the average success probability is independent of the rule used on tie sets. The code has now been reduced to its score covariance GG. We next change that covariance so that the regular simplex is represented by independent coordinates.

3.2 Adding a common Gaussian random variable

The variance of the added variable is determined by the simplex. For the regular-simplex Gram matrix, every off-diagonal entry equals −1/(m−1)-1/(m-1). Adding a common Gaussian variable of variance 1/(m−1)1/(m-1) therefore cancels those off-diagonal covariances, and a final rescaling restores unit marginal variances. We apply the same operation to every other Gram matrix competing with the simplex.

Set

α=m−1m.\alpha=\frac{m-1}{m}. (23)

For a correlation matrix GG, define

R=α​G+(1−α)​J=m−1m​G+1m​J.R=\alpha G+(1-\alpha)J=\frac{m-1}{m}G+\frac{1}{m}J. (24)

Then RR is a correlation matrix and R−J/m=α​G⪰0R-J/m=\alpha G\succeq 0. Conversely, if a correlation matrix RR satisfies R−J/m⪰0R-J/m\succeq 0, then

G=α−1​(R−1m​J)G=\alpha^{-1}\left(R-\frac{1}{m}J\right) (25)

is positive semidefinite with unit diagonal. Thus the hypothesis in Theorem 2.1 is exactly the image of the class of score covariance matrices. Furthermore G△G_{\triangle} is transformed to ImI_{m} under this mapping.

For a probabilistic interpretation of this transform let ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G) and let B∼𝒩⁡(0,1/(m−1))B\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/(m-1)) be independent. Define

Xi=α​(ξi+B),1≤i≤m.X_{i}=\sqrt{\alpha}\,(\xi_{i}+B),\qquad 1\leq i\leq m. (26)

Then X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R) since

Cov⁡(X)=α⁡(G+1m−1​J)=R.\operatorname{Cov}(X)=\alpha\left(G+\frac{1}{m-1}J\right)=R.

Because the same variable BB is added to every coordinate,

maxi⁡Xi=α​(maxi⁡ξi+B).\max_{i}X_{i}=\sqrt{\alpha}\left(\max_{i}\xi_{i}+B\right).

With λ=α​μ\lambda=\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mu, we therefore obtain

e−μ2/2𝔼eμ​maxi​Xi\displaystyle e^{-\mu^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\max_{i}X_{i}} =e−μ2/2𝔼eλ​maxi​ξi𝔼eλ​B\displaystyle=e^{-\mu^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda B}
=e−λ2/2𝔼eλ​maxi​ξi.\displaystyle=e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}. (27)
Remark 3.1 (Role of the semidefinite condition).

The condition R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m is equivalent to

u𝖳​R​u≥1m​(∑i=1mui)2(u∈ℝm).u^{\mathsf{T}}Ru\geq\frac{1}{m}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\right)^{2}\qquad(u\in\mathbb{R}^{m}). (28)

It does not impose an entrywise sign pattern: matrices in this class may have both positive and negative correlations, as Remark 2.2 shows. It records exactly that RR is the image of a score covariance under (24). The transformation may also change rank; for example, G△G_{\triangle} has rank m−1m-1, whereas its image ImI_{m} has full rank. Whenever the proof uses a Gram representation of the matrix in (25), we choose unit vectors in ℝrank⁡G\mathbb{R}^{\rank G}, so no ambient dimension must be fixed in advance.

The reduction is complete: by (22) and (27), the Weak Simplex Conjecture (Corollary 2.6) follows once Theorem 2.1 is proved for the covariance class R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m. The next section supplies the Gaussian product inequality used in that proof.

4 A Gaussian product inequality

The event {X≤c𝟏}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\} is a product of one-dimensional indicators 𝟏{Xi≤c}\mathbf{1}_{\{X_{i}\leq c\}}, so a Gaussian product inequality is a natural starting point. The key result we use is a Gaussian product inequality that applies to bounded log-concave factors that are centered with respect to the standard Gaussian measure. This centering hypothesis will be the only obstruction to using the indicators directly, and Section 5 will address how to resolve that obstruction.

A function f:ℝ→[0,∞)f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty) is log-concave if

f((1−θ)x+θy)≥f(x)1−θf(y)θ(x,y∈ℝ, 0≤θ≤1).f((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\geq f(x)^{1-\theta}f(y)^{\theta}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb{R},\ 0\leq\theta\leq 1).

We allow ff to vanish; in particular, indicators of intervals and the truncated exponentials used below are log-concave.

Lemma 4.1.

Let RR be an m×mm\times m correlation matrix and let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R). For each ii, let fi:ℝ→[0,∞)f_{i}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty) be bounded and log-concave, with positive Gaussian integral, and suppose that

∫ℝz​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}}zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0. (29)

Then

𝔼​∏i=1mfi​(Xi)≥∏i=1m𝔼​fi​(Xi)=∏i=1m∫ℝfi​d​γ1.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(X_{i})\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}f_{i}(X_{i})=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}. (30)

The covariance matrix RR may be singular.

To interpret (29), divide fif_{i} by its Gaussian integral. The measure

fi​d​γ1∫fi​d​γ1\frac{f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}}{\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}}

is then a probability measure, and (29) says precisely that this measure has mean zero. The lemma therefore compares the correlated product with the independent product under a coordinatewise centering condition.

The product inequality itself does not use the condition R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m from Theorem 2.1. That condition enters only in Section 5, where we need it to supply a Gram representation of α−1​(R−J/m)\alpha^{-1}(R-J/m).

Lemma 4.1 is a specialization of the Gaussian forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb theorem of Milman, Nakamura, and Tsuji [22, Theorem 1.10]. The exact parameter assignment is given in Section B.1. For self-containment, Appendix B also gives a direct proof of precisely this one-dimensional-factor specialization, using the Gaussian correlation inequality, normalized self-convolution, and the central limit theorem. The direct argument additionally supplies the strict form needed in Remark 2.3. Su et al. independently obtain the same strict product conclusion by strengthening the first self-convolution step with a Royen-based strict rectangle inequality [36, Sections V-A–V-B].

For the raw indicators, the two sides of the product inequality are already the two sides of (13). Indeed, for fi(z)=𝟏(−∞,c](z)f_{i}(z)=\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,c]}(z),

𝔼∏i=1mfi(Xi)=ℙ{X≤c𝟏},∏i=1m∫fidγ1=Φ(c)m.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(X_{i})=\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\},\qquad\prod_{i=1}^{m}\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}=\Phi(c)^{m}.

However, the required first moment is

∫z​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=−φ⁡(c)≠0.\int zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=-\varphi(c)\neq 0.

Multiplying by an exponential can restore the missing first moment, but the same weight shifts the mean of the multivariate Gaussian vector XX. The inequality (30) is therefore available only after the centering condition (29) has been reconciled with the target event {X≤c𝟏}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}. That compatibility problem is the subject of the next section.

5 Adaptive threshold alignment

Fix a target threshold c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. The raw indicators of the event {X≤c𝟏}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\} fail the centering hypothesis in Lemma 4.1. We therefore replace the iith indicator by a truncated exponential

fi(z)=eai​z𝟏(−∞,bi](z).f_{i}(z)=e^{a_{i}z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b_{i}]}(z).

The parameter aia_{i} must center the one-dimensional factor, while the endpoint bib_{i} must compensate for the joint Gaussian mean displacement R​aRa created by all the tilts. So our construction will have a one-dimensional part and a coupled part. We first derive the two required identities, then solve the one-dimensional centering equation, and finally choose all endpoints by a strictly concave variational problem.

5.1 Required conditions for the tilted factors

For vectors a∈(0,∞)ma\in(0,\infty)^{m} and b∈ℝmb\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, consider

fi(z)=eai​z𝟏(−∞,bi](z).f_{i}(z)=e^{a_{i}z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b_{i}]}(z). (31)

The Gaussian change-of-measure identity below describes the multivariate effect of these parameters. We include the short proof that also covers the singular covariance case.

Lemma 5.1.

Let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R) for a positive-semidefinite matrix RR. For every a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and every nonnegative Borel function F:ℝm→[0,∞]F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to[0,\infty],

𝔼⁡[ea𝖳​X​F​(X)]=e12​a𝖳​R​a​𝔼​F​(X+R​a).\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}F(X)\right]=e^{\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra}\mathbb{E}F(X+Ra). (32)
Proof.

Choose a matrix TT and a standard Gaussian vector Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) such that X=T​ZX=TZ and T​T𝖳=RTT^{\mathsf{T}}=R. With θ=T𝖳​a\theta=T^{\mathsf{T}}a, let φd\varphi_{d} denote the standard Gaussian density on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Completing the square gives

eθ𝖳​z−‖θ‖2/2​φd​(z)=φd​(z−θ).e^{\theta^{\mathsf{T}}z-\|\theta\|^{2}/2}\varphi_{d}(z)=\varphi_{d}(z-\theta).

A change of variables therefore yields

𝔼⁡[ea𝖳​X−12​a𝖳​R​a​F​(X)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X-\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra}F(X)\right] =𝔼⁡[eθ𝖳​Z−‖θ‖2/2​F​(T​Z)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{\theta^{\mathsf{T}}Z-\|\theta\|^{2}/2}F(TZ)\right]
=𝔼​F​(T⁡(Z+θ))=𝔼​F​(X+R​a),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}F(T(Z+\theta))=\mathbb{E}F(X+Ra),

which is equivalent to (32). ∎

Two identities are required. First, each coordinate must satisfy the centering hypothesis of Lemma 4.1:

∫ℝzeai​z𝟏(−∞,bi](z)dγ1(z)=0(1≤i≤m).\int_{\mathbb{R}}ze^{a_{i}z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b_{i}]}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0\qquad(1\leq i\leq m). (33)

Second, after the Gaussian change of measure, the weighted event must become the target event {X≤c𝟏}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}. Applying Lemma 5.1 with F(x)=𝟏{x≤b}F(x)=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\leq b\}} gives

𝔼[ea𝖳​X𝟏{X≤b}]=e12​a𝖳​R​aℙ{X≤b−Ra}.\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq b\}}\right]=e^{\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra}\mathbb{P}\{X\leq b-Ra\}.

We must therefore choose the endpoints so that

b−R​a=c​𝟏.b-Ra=c\mathbf{1}. (34)

Under this condition,

𝔼[ea𝖳​X𝟏{X≤b}]=e12​a𝖳​R​aℙ{X≤c𝟏}.\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq b\}}\right]=e^{\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra}\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}. (35)

Completing the square also gives the Gaussian integral of an individual factor:

∫−∞bieai​z​d​γ1​(z)=eai2/2​Φ​(bi−ai).\int_{-\infty}^{b_{i}}e^{a_{i}z}\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=e^{a_{i}^{2}/2}\Phi(b_{i}-a_{i}).

Consequently, once (33) and (34) hold, Lemma 4.1 and (35) give

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}≥exp(12a𝖳(Im−R)a)∏i=1mΦ(bi−ai).\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}\geq\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a\right)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\Phi(b_{i}-a_{i}). (36)

It remains to choose aa and bb so that both required identities hold and

exp⁡(12​a𝖳​(Im−R)​a)​∏i=1mΦ⁡(bi−ai)≥Φ​(c)m.\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a\right)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\Phi(b_{i}-a_{i})\geq\Phi(c)^{m}. (37)

Section 5.2 solves the one-dimensional centering condition and identifies the potential used to couple the coordinates. Section 5.3 then enforces threshold compatibility and proves (37) simultaneously.

5.2 The one-dimensional centered factors

The first condition in (33) is one-dimensional and can be solved explicitly. For a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}, let fa,b(z)=ea​z𝟏(−∞,b](z)f_{a,b}(z)=e^{az}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b]}(z) and set

s=b−a.s=b-a.

ss will allow us to parameterize the family of fa,bf_{a,b} satisfying (33).

Lemma 5.2.

For a,b,sa,b,s as above,

∫fa,b​d​γ1\displaystyle\int f_{a,b}\,d\gamma_{1} =ea2/2​Φ​(s),\displaystyle=e^{a^{2}/2}\Phi(s), (38)
∫z​fa,b​(z)​d​γ1​(z)\displaystyle\int zf_{a,b}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z) =ea2/2​(a​Φ​(s)−φ⁡(s)).\displaystyle=e^{a^{2}/2}\bigl(a\Phi(s)-\varphi(s)\bigr). (39)

a=r⁡(s):=φ⁡(s)Φ⁡(s),b=H⁡(s):=s+r⁡(s).a=r(s):=\frac{\varphi(s)}{\Phi(s)},\qquad b=H(s):=s+r(s). (40)
Proof.

The identity ea​z​φ​(z)=ea2/2​φ​(z−a)e^{az}\varphi(z)=e^{a^{2}/2}\varphi(z-a) gives (38). Differentiating that identity with respect to aa while keeping bb fixed gives (39). Since Φ⁡(s)>0\Phi(s)>0, the last assertion follows by solving a​Φ​(s)−φ⁡(s)=0a\Phi(s)-\varphi(s)=0. ∎

Thus a single parameter ss determines both the tilt and the endpoint. For Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),

r⁡(s)=−𝔼⁡[Z∣Z≤s],H⁡(s)=𝔼⁡[s−Z∣Z≤s],r(s)=-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Z\leq s],\qquad H(s)=\mathbb{E}[s-Z\mid Z\leq s],

The coupled construction is most conveniently written in terms of the endpoint b=H⁡(s)b=H(s). We therefore introduce a potential whose derivative with respect to bb is the required tilt. Along the centered family, define

ℱ(H(s))=log∫fr⁡(s),H⁡(s)dγ1=logΦ(s)+12r(s)2.\mathcal{F}(H(s))=\log\!\int f_{r(s),H(s)}\,d\gamma_{1}=\log\Phi(s)+\frac{1}{2}r(s)^{2}. (41)

dd​s​ℱ​(H⁡(s))=r⁡(s)+r⁡(s)​r′​(s)=r⁡(s)​H′​(s),\frac{d}{ds}\mathcal{F}(H(s))=r(s)+r(s)r^{\prime}(s)=r(s)H^{\prime}(s),

Proposition 5.3.

The function rr is a strictly decreasing bijection from ℝ\mathbb{R} onto (0,∞)(0,\infty), and HH is a strictly increasing bijection from ℝ\mathbb{R} onto (0,∞)(0,\infty). The function ℱ:(0,∞)→(−∞,0)\mathcal{F}:(0,\infty)\to(-\infty,0) defined by (41) is a strictly increasing, strictly concave bijection. Moreover,

ℱ′​(H⁡(s))=r⁡(s)(s∈ℝ).\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(H(s))=r(s)\qquad(s\in\mathbb{R}). (42)

Because rr and HH are bijective, the centered family (s,a,b)=(s,r⁡(s),H⁡(s))(s,a,b)=(s,r(s),H(s)) can be parametrized by s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, by the tilt a>0a>0, or by the endpoint b>0b>0. The endpoint parametrization is useful because (34) is an equation for bb.

5.3 Deriving the variational problem

Apply rr and HH coordinatewise and write ai=r⁡(si)a_{i}=r(s_{i}) and bi=H⁡(si)b_{i}=H(s_{i}). Then the factors in (31) satisfy the centering condition for every s∈ℝms\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. For an endpoint bi=H⁡(si)b_{i}=H(s_{i}), the corresponding tilt is ai=r⁡(si)=ℱ′​(bi)a_{i}=r(s_{i})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(b_{i}). Thus (34) is the fixed-point equation

b=c​𝟏+R​a=c​𝟏+R​ℱ′​(b),b=c\mathbf{1}+Ra=c\mathbf{1}+R\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(b), (43)

where ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is applied coordinatewise and b∈(0,∞)mb\in(0,\infty)^{m}.

The semidefinite condition R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m now enters. Recall α=(m−1)/m\alpha=(m-1)/m and set

G=α−1​(R−1m​J).G=\alpha^{-1}\left(R-\frac{1}{m}J\right).

Then GG is a correlation matrix. Choose unit vectors x1,…,xm∈ℝdx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, with d=rank⁡Gd=\rank G, such that Gi​j=⟨xi,xj⟩G_{ij}=\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle. For any a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, let a¯=m−1​∑iai\bar{a}=m^{-1}\sum_{i}a_{i}. Since R=α​G+J/mR=\alpha G+J/m,

(R​a)i=α⁡⟨xi,∑j=1maj​xj⟩+a¯.(Ra)_{i}=\alpha\langle x_{i},\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}x_{j}\rangle+\bar{a}. (44)

This decomposition suggests the variables in which to solve (43). Put

v=∑j=1maj​xj,q=c+a¯.v=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}x_{j},\qquad q=c+\bar{a}.

Then (43) is equivalent to

bi=q+α⁡⟨xi,v⟩,q−c=1m​∑i=1mai,v=∑i=1mai​xi.b_{i}=q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle,\qquad q-c=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i},\qquad v=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}x_{i}. (45)

on the open convex set

𝒟={(q,v):q+α⁡⟨xi,v⟩>0​ for every ​i}.\mathcal{D}=\left\{(q,v):q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle>0\text{ for every }i\right\}. (47)

The domain is nonempty because (q,0)∈𝒟(q,0)\in\mathcal{D} whenever q>0q>0. If bi=q+α⁡⟨xi,v⟩b_{i}=q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle and ai=ℱ′​(bi)a_{i}=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(b_{i}), then

∂q𝒥c​(q,v)\displaystyle\partial_{q}\mathcal{J}_{c}(q,v) =∑i=1mai−m⁡(q−c),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}-m(q-c), (48)

Setting these gradients to zero gives the last two equations in (45). Therefore, with bi=q+α⁡⟨xi,v⟩b_{i}=q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle and ai=ℱ′​(bi)a_{i}=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(b_{i}), every stationary point of 𝒥c\mathcal{J}_{c} satisfies b−R​a=c​𝟏b-Ra=c\mathbf{1}.

The value of the same functional supplies the probability estimate. At a stationary point,

α2​‖v‖2+m2​(q−c)2=12​a𝖳​R​a,\frac{\alpha}{2}\|v\|^{2}+\frac{m}{2}(q-c)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra,

while (41) gives ℱ⁡(bi)=log⁡Φ⁡(si)+ai2/2\mathcal{F}(b_{i})=\log\Phi(s_{i})+a_{i}^{2}/2. Hence 𝒥c​(q,v)\mathcal{J}_{c}(q,v) is precisely the logarithm of the lower bound in (36). The symmetric trial point (H⁡(c),0)(H(c),0) satisfies

𝒥c​(H⁡(c),0)=m​ℱ​(H⁡(c))−m2​r​(c)2=m​log⁡Φ⁡(c).\mathcal{J}_{c}(H(c),0)=m\mathcal{F}(H(c))-\frac{m}{2}r(c)^{2}=m\log\Phi(c).

Thus a maximizer of 𝒥c\mathcal{J}_{c} yields both the compatible endpoints and the benchmark in (37). The next theorem establishes existence and uniqueness and records these two outputs.

Theorem 5.4.

For every c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, the functional 𝒥c\mathcal{J}_{c} has a unique maximizer (q∗,v∗)∈𝒟(q_{*},v_{*})\in\mathcal{D}. There are unique s∗,i∈ℝs_{*,i}\in\mathbb{R} such that

H⁡(s∗,i)=q∗+α⁡⟨xi,v∗⟩.H(s_{*,i})=q_{*}+\alpha\langle x_{i},v_{*}\rangle.

Define

a∗,i=r⁡(s∗,i),b∗,i=H⁡(s∗,i)=s∗,i+a∗,i.a_{*,i}=r(s_{*,i}),\qquad b_{*,i}=H(s_{*,i})=s_{*,i}+a_{*,i}.

Then

b∗−R​a∗=c​𝟏b_{*}-Ra_{*}=c\mathbf{1} (50)

and

∑i=1mlog⁡Φ⁡(s∗,i)+12​a∗𝖳​(Im−R)​a∗≥m​log⁡Φ⁡(c).\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Phi(s_{*,i})+\frac{1}{2}a_{*}^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a_{*}\geq m\log\Phi(c). (51)
Proof.

Each term involving ℱ\mathcal{F} in (46) is concave, while the two negative quadratic terms are jointly strictly concave. Hence 𝒥c\mathcal{J}_{c} is strictly concave. Moreover, ℱ<0\mathcal{F}<0 and negativity of the quadratic terms imply 𝒥c​(q,v)→−∞\mathcal{J}_{c}(q,v)\to-\infty as ‖(q,v)‖→∞\|(q,v)\|\to\infty, whereas ℱ⁡(y)→−∞\mathcal{F}(y)\to-\infty as y↓0y\downarrow 0 implies that 𝒥c\mathcal{J}_{c} tends to −∞-\infty at the boundary of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Its nonempty upper level sets are therefore compact subsets of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. A maximizer exists, and strict concavity makes it unique.

Set

b∗,i=q∗+α⁡⟨xi,v∗⟩=H⁡(s∗,i),a∗,i=ℱ′​(b∗,i)=r⁡(s∗,i)>0.b_{*,i}=q_{*}+\alpha\langle x_{i},v_{*}\rangle=H(s_{*,i}),\qquad a_{*,i}=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(b_{*,i})=r(s_{*,i})>0.

The stationarity equations (48) give

v∗=∑i=1ma∗,i​xi,q∗=c+a¯∗,a¯∗=1m​∑i=1ma∗,i.v_{*}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{*,i}x_{i},\qquad q_{*}=c+\bar{a}_{*},\qquad\bar{a}_{*}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{*,i}. (52)

Combining (44) and (52),

(R​a∗)i=α⁡⟨xi,v∗⟩+a¯∗,(Ra_{*})_{i}=\alpha\langle x_{i},v_{*}\rangle+\bar{a}_{*},

and therefore

b∗,i=q∗+α⁡⟨xi,v∗⟩=c+(R​a∗)i.b_{*,i}=q_{*}+\alpha\langle x_{i},v_{*}\rangle=c+(Ra_{*})_{i}.

This proves (50).

At the maximizer,

∑i=1mℱ⁡(b∗,i)=∑i=1mlog⁡Φ⁡(s∗,i)+12​‖a∗‖2.\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{F}(b_{*,i})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Phi(s_{*,i})+\frac{1}{2}\|a_{*}\|^{2}.

Moreover, (52) gives

a∗𝖳​R​a∗\displaystyle a_{*}^{\mathsf{T}}Ra_{*} =α​‖∑i=1ma∗,i​xi‖2+1m​(∑i=1ma∗,i)2\displaystyle=\alpha\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{*,i}x_{i}\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{m}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{*,i}\right)^{2}
=α​‖v∗‖2+m​(q∗−c)2.\displaystyle=\alpha\|v_{*}\|^{2}+m(q_{*}-c)^{2}.

Consequently,

𝒥c​(q∗,v∗)=∑i=1mlog⁡Φ⁡(s∗,i)+12​a∗𝖳​(Im−R)​a∗.\mathcal{J}_{c}(q_{*},v_{*})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Phi(s_{*,i})+\frac{1}{2}a_{*}^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a_{*}. (53)

Finally,

𝒥c​(H​(c),0)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{c}(H(c),0) =m⁡(log⁡Φ⁡(c)+12​r​(c)2)−m2​(H⁡(c)−c)2\displaystyle=m\left(\log\Phi(c)+\frac{1}{2}r(c)^{2}\right)-\frac{m}{2}(H(c)-c)^{2}
=m⁡(log⁡Φ⁡(c)+12​r​(c)2)−m2​r​(c)2\displaystyle=m\left(\log\Phi(c)+\frac{1}{2}r(c)^{2}\right)-\frac{m}{2}r(c)^{2}
=m​log⁡Φ​(c).\displaystyle=m\log\Phi(c).

Maximality and (53) prove (51). ∎

Theorem 5.4 has produced exactly the vectors aa and bb required by (33) and (34), together with the scalar estimate needed in (37). The semidefinite hypothesis R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m is used precisely in this construction: it makes G=α−1​(R−J/m)G=\alpha^{-1}(R-J/m) positive semidefinite and hence provides the Gram representation in (44). No inverse of RR is used, so the argument applies without change when RR is singular.

6 Proof of the stochastic comparison

At this point the construction is complete. The product inequality bounds the weighted lower-orthant event, the Gaussian change of measure removes the weight, and the variational theorem supplies both the common threshold and the remaining scalar estimate. Their combination proves Theorem 2.1.

Proof of the stochastic comparison in Theorem 2.1.

Let R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m, let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R), and fix c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. Take s∈ℝms\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and a,b∈(0,∞)ma,b\in(0,\infty)^{m} from Theorem 5.4. For 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, define univariate functions

fi(z)=eai​z𝟏(−∞,bi](z).f_{i}(z)=e^{a_{i}z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b_{i}]}(z).

These functions are bounded and log-concave, and Lemma 5.2 gives

∫z​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0,∫fi​d​γ1=eai2/2​Φ​(si).\int zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0,\qquad\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}=e^{a_{i}^{2}/2}\Phi(s_{i}).

Applying Lemma 4.1 yields

𝔼[ea𝖳​X𝟏{X≤b}]≥e‖a‖2/2∏i=1mΦ(si).\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq b\}}\right]\geq e^{\|a\|^{2}/2}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\Phi(s_{i}). (54)

On the other hand, (50) and Lemma 5.1 give the event identity

𝔼[ea𝖳​X𝟏{X≤b}]=ea𝖳​R​a/2ℙ{X≤c𝟏}.\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq b\}}\right]=e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra/2}\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}. (55)

The quotient of the two Gaussian normalizing factors is therefore exp⁡{a𝖳​(Im−R)​a/2}\exp\{a^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a/2\}, exactly the quadratic term in the variational bound. Combining (54) and (55), and then applying (51),

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\} ≥exp⁡(12​a𝖳​(Im−R)​a)​∏i=1mΦ⁡(si)\displaystyle\geq\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a\right)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\Phi(s_{i})
=exp⁡(∑i=1mlog⁡Φ⁡(si)+12​a𝖳​(Im−R)​a)\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Phi(s_{i})+\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I_{m}-R)a\right)
≥Φ​(c)m.\displaystyle\geq\Phi(c)^{m}.

Since cc was arbitrary, this proves 𝖬X≤st𝖬Z\mathsf{M}_{X}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\mathsf{M}_{Z}. ∎

If R=ImR=I_{m}, then equality in distribution is immediate. If R≠ImR\neq I_{m}, the strict refinement in Theorem B.6 gives

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}>Φ(c)m(c∈ℝ),\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}>\Phi(c)^{m}\qquad(c\in\mathbb{R}),

so the laws of 𝖬X\mathsf{M}_{X} and 𝖬Z\mathsf{M}_{Z} are different. This proves the equality statement in Theorem 2.1.

The stochastic comparison, including its equality statement, is now complete.

7 Applications

Theorem 2.1 compares the maximum associated with the transformed covariance RR to the independent Gaussian maximum. The applications require two further steps. First, stochastic order must be converted into expectation inequalities. Second, (24) and (27) must be used to return from RR to the original score covariance GG. We carry this out first for Gaussian maxima and classification, then extend the expected-maximum comparison to covariance matrices with marginal variances at most one, and finally treat the finite-energy AWGN sequence model.

7.1 Increasing functions of the normalized maximum

Proof of Corollary 2.4.

For a real random variable UU, let

QU(u)=inf{x∈ℝ:ℙ{U≤x}≥u},0<u<1,Q_{U}(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}:\mathbb{P}\{U\leq x\}\geq u\},\qquad 0<u<1,

be its generalized quantile function. If WW is uniform on (0,1)(0,1), then Q𝖬X​(W)Q_{\mathsf{M}_{X}}(W) and Q𝖬Z​(W)Q_{\mathsf{M}_{Z}}(W) have the laws of 𝖬X\mathsf{M}_{X} and 𝖬Z\mathsf{M}_{Z}. The stochastic order in Theorem 2.1 is equivalent to

Q𝖬X​(u)≤Q𝖬Z​(u)(0<u<1).Q_{\mathsf{M}_{X}}(u)\leq Q_{\mathsf{M}_{Z}}(u)\qquad(0<u<1).

Applying a nondecreasing nonnegative function ψ\psi and then taking expectations proves the first assertion, including the case of infinite expectations.

If R≠ImR\neq I_{m}, the equality statement in Theorem 2.1 shows that the two maximum laws are different. Their quantile functions therefore differ on a set of positive Lebesgue measure. For a strictly increasing ψ\psi, the inequality

ψ⁡(Q𝖬X​(W))≤ψ⁡(Q𝖬Z​(W))\psi(Q_{\mathsf{M}_{X}}(W))\leq\psi(Q_{\mathsf{M}_{Z}}(W))

is then strict with positive probability. Integrability yields the strict expectation inequality. Gaussian maxima have finite moments and finite positive exponential moments of every order, so the choices ψ⁡(x)=x\psi(x)=x and ψ⁡(x)=eλ​x\psi(x)=e^{\lambda x} give the final statements. ∎

7.2 Returning to the score covariance

Let GG be a correlation matrix, let ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G), and define RR and XX by (24) and (26). The stochastic comparison acts on maxi⁡Xi\max_{i}X_{i}, but the normalized identity (27) transfers every positive exponential moment exactly back to maxi⁡ξi\max_{i}\xi_{i}. This is precisely the transfer needed for the decoding objective.

Proof of Corollary 2.5.

Fix λ>0\lambda>0 and set μ=λ/α\mu=\lambda/\sqrt{\alpha}. By Corollary 2.4,

𝔼​eμ​maxi​Xi≤𝔼​eμ​𝖬Z,\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\max_{i}X_{i}}\leq\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\mathsf{M}_{Z}},

with strict inequality unless R=ImR=I_{m}. Apply (27) to GG. Applying the same identity to G△G_{\triangle}, whose transformed covariance is ImI_{m}, converts the right-hand side into the regular-simplex score maximum. The common factor e−λ2/2e^{-\lambda^{2}/2} cancels, giving (16). Finally, R=ImR=I_{m} if and only if G=G△G=G_{\triangle}, so the strict comparison gives the stated equality characterization. ∎

The maximum-likelihood identity now turns the Gaussian MGF comparison into the coding theorem without any additional estimate.

Proof of Corollary 2.6.

Let GG be the Gram matrix of the code. By (22), its correct-decoding probability is

e−λ2/2m​𝔼​exp⁡{λ​maxi​ξi}.\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}\right\}.

The prefactor is independent of the code, so Corollary 2.5 proves maximality of G△G_{\triangle}. When m=d+1m=d+1, this matrix is realized by a regular simplex in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Equality at the fixed positive signal strength forces G=G△G=G_{\triangle}.

The matrix G△G_{\triangle} has rank dd, so any ordered configuration with this Gram matrix spans ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Two spanning ordered configurations with the same Gram matrix differ by an orthogonal transformation. Since relabeling the vertices leaves G△G_{\triangle} unchanged, this gives uniqueness up to orthogonal congruence and relabeling. ∎

7.3 Expected maxima under marginal variance constraints

For expected maxima, unlike positive exponential moments, the common Gaussian variable disappears after taking expectations. Moreover, points in a unit ball produce Gaussian coordinates whose variances may be strictly smaller than one. The following elementary variance-completion step bridges that gap.

Lemma 7.1 (Variance completion).

Let SS be an m×mm\times m positive-semidefinite matrix with Si​i≤1S_{ii}\leq 1, and let Y∼𝒩⁡(0,S)Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,S). Define

D=diag⁡(1−S11,…,1−Sm​m),D=\diag(1-S_{11},\ldots,1-S_{mm}),

and let W∼𝒩⁡(0,D)W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,D) be independent of YY. Then G=S+DG=S+D is a correlation matrix and

𝔼​maxi​Yi≤𝔼​maxi⁡(Yi+Wi).\mathbb{E}\max_{i}Y_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}(Y_{i}+W_{i}). (56)
Proof.

The matrix DD is positive semidefinite, so G=S+DG=S+D is positive semidefinite; its diagonal entries are one. For each realization of YY, convexity of the maximum gives the conditional Jensen inequality

maxi⁡Yi=maxi⁡𝔼⁡[Yi+Wi∣Y]≤𝔼⁡[maxi⁡(Yi+Wi)∣Y].\max_{i}Y_{i}=\max_{i}\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}+W_{i}\mid Y]\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{i}(Y_{i}+W_{i})\mid Y\right].

Taking expectations proves (56). ∎

Proof of Corollary 2.7.

We first prove the Gaussian statement. Apply Lemma 7.1 and write Y~=Y+W∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\widetilde{Y}=Y+W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G). The common-Gaussian representation (26), together with 𝔼​B=0\mathbb{E}B=0, gives

𝔼​𝖬X=α​𝔼​maxi​Y~i\mathbb{E}\mathsf{M}_{X}=\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\widetilde{Y}_{i} (57)

for the transformed covariance associated with GG. The same identity for G△G_{\triangle} gives

𝔼​𝖬Z=α​𝔼​maxi​ξi△.\mathbb{E}\mathsf{M}_{Z}=\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}.

The expectation comparison in Corollary 2.4 therefore yields

𝔼​maxi​Yi≤𝔼​maxi​Y~i≤𝔼​maxi​ξi△.\mathbb{E}\max_{i}Y_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\widetilde{Y}_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}.

Since the transformed covariance of G△G_{\triangle} is ImI_{m}, the preceding identity also gives

𝔼maxiξi△=α−1/2𝔼𝖬Z=mm−1𝔼maxiZi,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}=\alpha^{-1/2}\mathbb{E}\mathsf{M}_{Z}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}\,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}Z_{i},

which proves (17).

It remains to identify equality. If equality holds in (17), then the second inequality in the preceding chain is an equality. The strict part of Corollary 2.4 therefore forces G=G△G=G_{\triangle}. Since DD is diagonal, this already gives

Si​j=−1m−1(i≠j).S_{ij}=-\frac{1}{m-1}\qquad(i\neq j).

Positive semidefiniteness of SS and the bounds Si​i≤1S_{ii}\leq 1 imply

0≤𝟏𝖳​S​𝟏=∑i=1mSi​i+2​∑i<jSi​j=∑i=1mSi​i−m≤0.0\leq\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{ii}+2\sum_{i<j}S_{ij}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{ii}-m\leq 0.

Thus Si​i=1S_{ii}=1 for every ii, so D=0D=0 and S=G△S=G_{\triangle}. Conversely, S=G△S=G_{\triangle} clearly gives equality.

Now let y1,…,ymy_{1},\ldots,y_{m} lie in the Euclidean unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and put K=conv⁡{y1,…,ym}K=\conv\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\}. If g∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), then the Gaussian vector Yi=⟨g,yi⟩Y_{i}=\langle g,y_{i}\rangle has covariance S=(⟨yi,yj⟩)S=(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle), which is positive semidefinite with Si​i≤1S_{ii}\leq 1. Hence

𝔼​hK​(g)=𝔼​maxi​⟨g,yi⟩≤𝔼​maxi​ξi△.\mathbb{E}h_{K}(g)=\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\langle g,y_{i}\rangle\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}.

Let σd−1\sigma_{d-1} be normalized rotation-invariant measure on Sd−1S^{d-1} and use the convention

w⁡(K)=∫Sd−1(hK​(u)+hK​(−u))​d​σd−1​(u)=2​∫Sd−1hK​(u)​d​σd−1​(u).w(K)=\int_{S^{d-1}}\bigl(h_{K}(u)+h_{K}(-u)\bigr)\,d\sigma_{d-1}(u)=2\int_{S^{d-1}}h_{K}(u)\,d\sigma_{d-1}(u).

Writing gg as the product of its norm and its independent uniform direction gives

𝔼​hK​(g)=𝔼​∥g∥2​w​(K).\mathbb{E}h_{K}(g)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\lVert g\rVert}{2}\,w(K). (58)

Thus the Gaussian expected-maximum inequality is exactly the desired mean-width inequality in a fixed ambient dimension. Equality forces the Gram matrix of the yiy_{i} to be G△G_{\triangle}, so the points lie on the unit sphere and form a centered regular simplex. When d≥m−1d\geq m-1, such a simplex is feasible, and equal Gram matrices give uniqueness up to an orthogonal map on their spans, extended to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and relabeling. ∎

7.4 Finite-energy AWGN codes

The variance-completion argument above is sufficient for expected maxima, but it does not by itself solve the finite-energy decoding problem. When the codeword norms are unequal, the Gaussian likelihood scores contain the deterministic offsets −∥ci∥2/N0-\|c_{i}\|^{2}/N_{0} in addition to their random linear parts. The maximal per-codeword energy constraint nevertheless permits an exact reduction to the equal-energy setting. Because the sequence model also requires a measure-theoretic finite-dimensional reduction, we give the full details in Appendix E and retain here the structure of the argument.

Proof of Corollary 2.8.

The sufficient-statistic construction in Appendix E shows that every MM-message code in the AWGN sequence model is equivalent, for optimal decoding, to a Gaussian shift experiment of dimension at most M−1M-1. Next, one extra signal/noise coordinate is appended to replace each codeword cic_{i} by

c~i=(ci,E−∥ci∥2).\widetilde{c}_{i}=\left(c_{i},\sqrt{E-\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}}\right).

All augmented codewords have squared norm EE, and a decoder may ignore the new coordinate, so this operation cannot reduce the optimal success probability. Projecting away their common component orthogonal to the difference span leaves an equal-radius configuration in dimension at most M−1M-1. After embedding that span in ℝM−1\mathbb{R}^{M-1}, Corollary 2.6 bounds the configuration by a regular simplex of the same radius. Finally, a Gaussian degradation argument shows that the optimal success probability for a regular simplex is nondecreasing in its radius, so the full radius E\sqrt{E} is optimal. These reductions are formalized in Proposition E.1. Su et al. track equality through this chain to obtain the optimizer characterization stated after Corollary 2.8 [36, Theorem 3(b)].

To evaluate the optimum, translate the centered regular simplex to the orthogonal representatives A​eiAe_{i}, where A=E​M/(M−1)A=\sqrt{EM/(M-1)}. Translation by a common vector does not change any likelihood ratio. Conditioning on the noise in the transmitted coordinate then gives

Pc∗​(E,M)=𝔼​Φ​(W+2​E​M(M−1)​N0)M−1,W∼𝒩⁡(0,1),P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M)=\mathbb{E}\Phi\!\left(W+\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right)^{M-1},\qquad W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),

which is (19). The definition of M∗​(E,ϵ)M^{*}(E,\epsilon) now gives (20). As proved in Appendix E, pMp_{M} is continuous and strictly increasing, with pM​(0)=1/Mp_{M}(0)=1/M and pM​(a)↑1p_{M}(a)\uparrow 1. Inverting (19) therefore gives (21), including the endpoint cases ϵ≥1−1/M\epsilon\geq 1-1/M and ϵ=0\epsilon=0. ∎

The conclusion is specific to deterministic, equiprobable, no-feedback codes under a maximal per-codeword total-energy constraint, with no restriction on the number of channel uses. It proves the fixed-(M,ϵ)(M,\epsilon) simplex-code assertion discussed in [28, Remark 21.2]. Average energy over the codebook, feedback, unequal priors, and non-Gaussian noise are not covered by this reduction.

This completes the applications stated in Section 2. We close by recording the equality-case question posed in version 1, now resolved, followed by three further open problems.

8 A resolved problem and further questions

The first version of this paper posed the following question.

Problem 8.1 (Equality cases—resolved).

Determine the equality cases in (13), (16), and the coding and mean-width consequences. In particular, determine when equality at one nontrivial threshold or one positive MGF parameter forces R=ImR=I_{m}, or equivalently forces the original covariance to be G△G_{\triangle} after (24).

This statement appeared as Open Problem 8.1 in version 1. It was resolved independently by the present author and by Su et al. [36]. The present manuscript proves the stronger pointwise statement in Theorem B.6; Corollaries 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7 give the corresponding MGF, coding, and mean-width rigidity statements. We retain the statement and number as a historical resolved problem to preserve the referent in the title of [36]. The chronology and the relation between the two proof routes are described in Section 1.2.

The common-threshold comparison also isolates several nearby problems for which the present proof supplies only an upper bound or a counterexample to the most naive extension.

Open problem 8.2 (The rank-constrained Gaussian maximum).

Fix integers m≥3m\geq 3 and 1≤d<m−11\leq d<m-1, and fix λ>0\lambda>0. Determine

max{𝔼exp(λmax1≤i≤mξi):ξ∼𝒩(0,G),G a correlation matrix,rankG≤d},\max\left\{\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left(\lambda\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\xi_{i}\right):\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G),\ G\text{ a correlation matrix},\ \rank G\leq d\right\},

and characterize all maximizing covariance matrices. In particular, determine whether the maximizing configuration depends on λ\lambda.

The feasible set is compact, so a maximizer exists. Corollary 2.5 gives the regular (m−1)(m-1)-simplex value as a universal upper bound, but that covariance has rank m−1m-1 and is not feasible. Thus this problem asks for the optimal overloaded equal-energy Gaussian code when the number of signals exceeds the ambient dimension plus one. The unconstrained theorem does not indicate which boundary point of the rank-constrained elliptope should be optimal, so even the candidate geometry remains to be identified.

Open problem 8.3 (Universal lower-orthant thresholds).

Determine all vectors t=(t1,…,tm)∈ℝmt=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} for which

ℙ{Xi≤ti for every i}≥∏i=1mΦ(ti)\mathbb{P}\{X_{i}\leq t_{i}\text{ for every }i\}\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\Phi(t_{i})

holds for every correlation matrix R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m and every X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R).

Theorem 2.1 shows that every constant vector t=c​𝟏t=c\mathbf{1} has this property, whereas Remark 2.2 shows that arbitrary threshold vectors do not. A solution would identify the precise reach of the common-threshold phenomenon. It would also clarify whether the adaptive centering construction can be modified to treat any genuinely asymmetric family of one-sided events.

Open problem 8.4 (Average-energy Gaussian codes).

For fixed MM, ambient dimension, noise level, and average-energy budget EE, maximize the average probability of correct decoding over equiprobable Gaussian codebooks satisfying

1M​∑i=1M∥ci∥2≤E.\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E.

Characterize the optimizers as a function of the signal-to-noise ratio. Can an optimizer always be chosen from a family consisting of a lower-dimensional regular simplex together with coincident zero signals, or are additional geometries unavoidable?

The regular simplex is not always optimal under this weaker constraint: this is the failure of the Strong Simplex Conjecture proved by Steiner [35]. The known counterexample literature already exhibits a substantial family of lower-dimensional degeneracies. In particular, Sun studied codebooks formed by a regular simplex on KK nonzero signals together with M−KM-K zero signals, as well as related circle-plus-zero configurations [38]. These results show that the failure is not confined to a single exceptional construction, but they do not give a general description of the global optimizer. The maximal per-codeword constraint used in Corollary 2.8 rules out precisely this redistribution of energy among messages.

Other extensions—including unequal priors, feedback, and non-Gaussian noise—change either the one-dimensional centering equations or the Gaussian change of measure and therefore require new ideas beyond the argument given here.

Appendix B Details on the Gaussian product inequality

This appendix first records how Lemma 4.1 follows from the general Gaussian forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb theorem in Section B.1. It then gives an alternate direct proof from the symmetric Gaussian rectangle inequality, normalized self-convolution, and the central limit theorem in the subsequent sections of Appendix B. The direct proof also yields the stronger strict inequality at every finite common threshold stated in Remark 2.3. More general centered Gaussian correlation and forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb inequalities appear in [24, 25, 22].

B.1 Specialization of the forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb theorem

Lemma 4.1 is a specialization of [22, Theorem 1.10]. In the notation of that theorem, take I=mI=m, ni=1n_{i}=1, ci=1c_{i}=1, and Σi=1\Sigma_{i}=1 for every input; take a single output with m1=mm_{1}=m, d1=1d_{1}=1, L1=IdℝmL_{1}=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}, Γ1=R\Gamma_{1}=R, and 𝒬=0\mathcal{Q}=0. Set h⁡(x)=∏i=1mfi​(xi)h(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(x_{i}). The pointwise hypothesis then holds with equality, and the centeredness condition is precisely (29).

The remaining Gaussian constant in this specialization is

supAi≥0,B⪰0diag⁡(A1,…,Am)⪰Bdet(Im+R​B)1/2∏i=1m(1+Ai)1/2.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}A_{i}\geq 0,\ B\succeq 0\\ \diag(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m})\succeq B\end{subarray}}\frac{\det(I_{m}+RB)^{1/2}}{\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1+A_{i})^{1/2}}. (63)

Writing A=diag⁡(A1,…,Am)A=\diag(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}) and using B⪯AB\preceq A, Loewner monotonicity of the determinant, Sylvester’s determinant identity, and Hadamard’s inequality give

det(Im+R​B)\displaystyle\det(I_{m}+RB) =det(Im+R1/2​B​R1/2)\displaystyle=\det(I_{m}+R^{1/2}BR^{1/2})
≤det(Im+R1/2​A​R1/2)\displaystyle\leq\det(I_{m}+R^{1/2}AR^{1/2})
=det(Im+A1/2​R​A1/2)\displaystyle=\det(I_{m}+A^{1/2}RA^{1/2})
≤∏i=1m(1+Ai),\displaystyle\leq\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1+A_{i}),

because Ri​i=1R_{ii}=1. Thus the constant in (63) is at most one; taking A=B=0A=B=0 shows that it is exactly one. The general theorem allows Γ1=R\Gamma_{1}=R to be singular, and hence gives (30) for every correlation matrix RR.

B.2 Symmetric rectangles and even functions

We begin with the classical Šidák–Khatri inequality in the form needed below [17, 33], together with its equality case for finite nondegenerate rectangles. For a recent refinement, see [1]. For self-containment, we provide a direct proof.

Lemma B.1.

Let V=(V1,…,Vm)V=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{m}) be a centered Gaussian vector with Var⁡(Vi)=1\operatorname{Var}(V_{i})=1 for every ii. For r1,…,rm∈[0,∞]r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\in[0,\infty],

ℙ{|Vi|≤ri for all i}≥∏i=1mℙ{|Z|≤ri},Z∼𝒩(0,1).\mathbb{P}\{|V_{i}|\leq r_{i}\text{ for all }i\}\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{P}\{|Z|\leq r_{i}\},\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). (64)

If 0<ri<∞0<r_{i}<\infty for every ii, then equality in (64) holds if and only if Cov⁡(V)=Im\operatorname{Cov}(V)=I_{m}.

Proof.

By monotone convergence, it is enough for the non-strict assertion to treat finite radii. We proceed by induction on mm and allow singular covariance matrices throughout. The case m=1m=1 is equality. For the induction step, write

T=Vm,W=(V1,…,Vm−1),β=Cov⁡(W,T),T=V_{m},\qquad W=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{m-1}),\qquad\beta=\operatorname{Cov}(W,T),

and set Y=W−β​TY=W-\beta T. The Gaussian vectors YY and TT are uncorrelated and therefore independent, even when the joint covariance is singular. With

A=∏i<m[−ri,ri],q(t)=ℙ{Y+βt∈A},A=\prod_{i<m}[-r_{i},r_{i}],\qquad q(t)=\mathbb{P}\{Y+\beta t\in A\},

symmetry of AA and YY makes qq even. The function qq is log-concave as well. Indeed, represent Y=L​Z′Y=LZ^{\prime} on its linear support, with Z′Z^{\prime} a standard Gaussian vector of the appropriate dimension. Then

q⁡(t)=∫𝟏A​(L​z+β​t)​d​γk​(z)q(t)=\int\mathbf{1}_{A}(Lz+\beta t)\,d\gamma_{k}(z)

for a suitable kk, and Prékopa’s theorem [29, 8] applies to the jointly log-concave integrand. Hence qq is nonincreasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty).

Let U=|T|U=|T|, and let U′U^{\prime} be an independent copy. The functions u↦q⁡(u)u\mapsto q(u) and u↦𝟏{u≤rm}u\mapsto\mathbf{1}_{\{u\leq r_{m}\}} are both nonincreasing, so

2Cov(q(U),𝟏{U≤rm})=𝔼[(q(U)−q(U′))(𝟏{U≤rm}−𝟏{U′≤rm})]≥0.\displaystyle 2\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(q(U),\mathbf{1}_{\{U\leq r_{m}\}}\right)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(q(U)-q(U^{\prime}))(\mathbf{1}_{\{U\leq r_{m}\}}-\mathbf{1}_{\{U^{\prime}\leq r_{m}\}})\right]\geq 0.

Consequently,

ℙ{V∈A×[−rm,rm]}\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\{V\in A\times[-r_{m},r_{m}]\} =𝔼q(T)𝟏{|T|≤rm}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}q(T)\mathbf{1}_{\{|T|\leq r_{m}\}}
≥𝔼q(T)ℙ{|Z|≤rm}.\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}q(T)\,\mathbb{P}\{|Z|\leq r_{m}\}.

The first factor on the right is the rectangle probability for WW, so the induction hypothesis proves (64).

It remains to prove strictness. Assume that every radius is finite and positive and that R:=Cov⁡(V)≠ImR:=\operatorname{Cov}(V)\neq I_{m}. After relabeling the coordinates, we may arrange that the vector β\beta above is nonzero. Choose δ>0\delta>0 so that [−2​δ,2​δ]m−1⊂A[-2\delta,2\delta]^{m-1}\subset A. For all sufficiently small |t||t|, ∥β​t∥∞≤δ\lVert\beta t\rVert_{\infty}\leq\delta, and hence {∥Y∥∞≤δ}⊆{Y+βt∈A}\{\lVert Y\rVert_{\infty}\leq\delta\}\subseteq\{Y+\beta t\in A\}. A centered Gaussian assigns positive mass to this neighborhood of the origin relative to its linear support, so q⁡(t)>0q(t)>0 for all sufficiently small |t||t|. On the other hand, choose j<mj<m with βj≠0\beta_{j}\neq 0. Then

q(t)≤ℙ{|Yj+βjt|≤rj}⟶0(|t|→∞).q(t)\leq\mathbb{P}\{|Y_{j}+\beta_{j}t|\leq r_{j}\}\longrightarrow 0\qquad(|t|\to\infty).

We can therefore choose 0<a<rm<b0<a<r_{m}<b such that q⁡(a)>q⁡(b)q(a)>q(b). Since U=|T|U=|T| has a strictly positive density on (0,∞)(0,\infty), the integrand in the preceding covariance identity is strictly positive on the event {U⁡<a,U′>​b}\{U<a,\ U^{\prime}>b\}, which has positive probability. Thus the last-coordinate inequality is strict, and so is (64). Conversely, when R=ImR=I_{m}, the coordinates are independent and equality is immediate. ∎

Remark B.2.

The equality statement can also be obtained from Nakamura and Tsuji’s two-set theorem [24, Theorem 1.3] with some additional effort; however, the direct argument above is shorter in the present setting. Su et al. independently prove the same strict rectangle statement by first isolating a strict bivariate gap and then using Royen’s Gaussian correlation theorem to group the remaining coordinate slabs [36, Lemma 9].

Lemma B.3.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma B.1, let g1,…,gm:ℝ→[0,∞)g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty) be bounded, even, and log-concave. Then

𝔼​∏i=1mgi​(Vi)≥∏i=1m∫gi​d​γ1.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}(V_{i})\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\int g_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}. (65)
Proof.

Each strict superlevel set of an even log-concave function on ℝ\mathbb{R} is an interval centered at the origin, possibly empty or unbounded. Then the layer-cake formula, Tonelli’s theorem, and Lemma B.1 give

𝔼​∏i=1mgi​(Vi)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}(V_{i}) =∫[0,∞)mℙ{gi(Vi)>ti for all i}dt1⋯dtm\displaystyle=\int_{[0,\infty)^{m}}\mathbb{P}\{g_{i}(V_{i})>t_{i}\text{ for all }i\}\,dt_{1}\cdots dt_{m}
≥∫[0,∞)m∏i=1mℙ{gi(Z)>ti}dt1⋯dtm\displaystyle\geq\int_{[0,\infty)^{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{P}\{g_{i}(Z)>t_{i}\}\,dt_{1}\cdots dt_{m}
=∏i=1m𝔼​gi​(Z).\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}g_{i}(Z).

∎

B.5 Strictness for the truncated exponential factors

Su et al. independently insert their Royen-based rectangle lemma into the same first sum–difference/self-convolution step to obtain the strict product inequality for the truncated exponential factors [36, Lemma 10]. The argument below instead uses the direct strict rectangle theorem Lemma B.1; after this strict first step, both proofs invoke the non-strict centered product inequality for the convolved factors.

Appendix C Rigidity of the independent Gaussian maximum law

The equality statement in Theorem 2.1 follows in the main text from the strict product inequality tailored to the truncated exponential factors. Dai and Mukherjea studied the broader identification problem for multivariate normal families with a common correlation parameter and also for a common-covariance family [10]. The proposition below treats a different comparison: equality with the independent standard maximum for an arbitrary covariance matrix, including singular matrices and unequal marginal variances.

Su et al. independently developed and machine-checked a related upper-tail rigidity route under the normalized correlation-matrix hypotheses of the main theorem [36, Remark 1]. Their route passes from stochastic domination and equality of one positive exponential moment to equality of the maximum laws, and then uses bivariate upper-tail asymptotics to force R=ImR=I_{m}; their formalization also proves Gram rigidity. The argument below was developed independently and requires neither unit marginal variances nor the semidefinite condition R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m.

Write Φ¯​(t)=1−Φ​(t)\overline{\Phi}(t)=1-\Phi(t).

Appendix D Relation to two prior announced proofs

Goldsmith [12] and Pastore [26] announce proofs of the Simplex Mean Width and Weak Simplex conjectures, respectively. We record why we do not use the current posted versions as prior proofs. The discussion concerns only arXiv:2112.03393v2, revised 27 June 2023, and arXiv:2306.13478v2, revised 13 November 2023. All page, section, theorem, and equation references below refer to those versions. It is not a claim that either conjecture is false, that either strategy cannot be repaired, or that the authors have no later argument.

D.1 Goldsmith’s centroid-monotonicity step

The dependency in [12] is

Theorem 3.1⟹Corollary 3.2⟹Theorem 4.1.\text{Theorem 3.1}\Longrightarrow\text{Corollary 3.2}\Longrightarrow\text{Theorem 4.1}.

Theorem 3.1 is a strict monotonicity statement for spherical centroids under a longitudinal shift. On pp. 7–9, its proof uses local approximations and reduces the pointwise Prékopa–Leindler hypothesis to a sufficient inequality. At the end of p. 9, the manuscript observes that this inequality fails as the dimension tends to infinity and derives only a restricted angular condition. The proof then ends without another estimate verifying the required pointwise hypothesis. Corollary 3.2 invokes Theorem 3.1, and Theorem 4.1 invokes Corollary 3.2. Thus the posted argument does not establish the claimed all-dimensional theorem.

D.2 Pastore’s centroid-injectivity step

The injectivity argument in Section III-D of [26] defines conditional means tt and t′t^{\prime} over the differences D~∖D~′\widetilde{D}\setminus\widetilde{D}^{\prime} and D~′∖D~\widetilde{D}^{\prime}\setminus\widetilde{D} in (18c)–(18d). The appendix obtains the set inclusions (23b)–(23c) and then treats the means as points of the corresponding differences when deriving the sign statements (24b)–(24c). A conditional mean belongs to the closed convex hull of its support, not necessarily to the support itself, and a difference of convex cones need not be convex. The failed inequality in (24b) or (24c) may depend on the sampled point and need not survive averaging.

The issue occurs within the Gaussian simplicial-cone setting. In ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} let

where a>0a>0. Then

Da′={x1>0,x2>a​x1,x3>a​x1}⊂D.D^{\prime}_{a}=\{x_{1}>0,\ x_{2}>ax_{1},\ x_{3}>ax_{1}\}\subset D.

Let Z∼𝒩⁡(0,I3)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{3}), put Aa=D∖Da′A_{a}=D\setminus D^{\prime}_{a}, and write Q=1−ΦQ=1-\Phi. Define

There is a second, independent issue in the same appendix. Appendix E Proof of the finite-energy AWGN corollary

We prove Corollary 2.8. The channel is the real AWGN sequence model

Y=X+Z,Zj∼iid𝒩⁡(0,N0/2).Y=X+Z,\qquad Z_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,N_{0}/2). (87)

The encoder is deterministic, the MM messages are equiprobable, there is no feedback, and every codeword ci∈ℓ2c_{i}\in\ell_{2} satisfies ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E. The decoder is arbitrary, and there is no constraint on the number of channel uses or nonzero codeword coordinates. This is the finite-energy model of [27, Definition 1].

The output sequence ZZ is almost surely not in ℓ2\ell_{2}, so the observation cannot be projected directly onto a finite-dimensional subspace of ℓ2\ell_{2}. Nevertheless, the likelihood ratios depend on finitely many Gaussian linear statistics. We construct those statistics first.
