supn𝔼P1​Li,n2≤exp⁡(2​∥di∥2N0)<∞.\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}_{P_{1}}L_{i,n}^{2}\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{2\lVert d_{i}\rVert^{2}}{N_{0}}\right)<\infty.

Hence Li,nL_{i,n} converges in L1​(P1)L^{1}(P_{1}) to the expression in (90). In particular, every likelihood ratio is measurable with respect to T=(T1,…,Tr)T=(T_{1},\ldots,T_{r}).

Let ℓ1≡1\ell_{1}\equiv 1 and let P¯=M−1​∑i=1MPi\overline{P}=M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{M}P_{i} be the output law under the uniform prior. Bayes’ formula gives

ℙ⁡{I=i∣Y}=ℓi​(T​(Y))∑k=1Mℓk​(T⁡(Y))P¯​-almost surely.\mathbb{P}\{I=i\mid Y\}=\frac{\ell_{i}(T(Y))}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\ell_{k}(T(Y))}\qquad\overline{P}\text{-almost surely}. (92)

Thus a Bayes-optimal decoder, equivalently a maximum-likelihood decoder under the uniform prior, is a function of TT. Conversely, every decoder based on TT is also available in the full experiment. The sequence model and the finite-dimensional Gaussian model in (89) therefore have the same optimal probability of correct decoding.

E.2 Optimality of a full-energy regular simplex

Proposition E.1.

Among all MM-message codes in the preceding model, the optimal average probability of correct decoding is attained by a centered regular (M−1)(M-1)-simplex whose vertices have squared norm EE.

Proof.

Start with arbitrary codewords c1,…,cM∈ℓ2c_{1},\ldots,c_{M}\in\ell_{2} satisfying ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E. Append one independent signal/noise coordinate; after relabeling the countable coordinates, this is the isometric embedding ℓ2↪ℓ2⊕ℝ≅ℓ2\ell_{2}\hookrightarrow\ell_{2}\oplus\mathbb{R}\cong\ell_{2}. Set

c~i=(ci,E−∥ci∥2).\widetilde{c}_{i}=\left(c_{i},\sqrt{E-\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}}\right). (93)

Every augmented codeword has squared norm EE. A decoder in the augmented experiment may ignore the additional observation coordinate and use the original decoder. Thus optimal correct-decoding probability cannot decrease under this augmentation.

Let

D~=span⁡{c~i−c~1:1≤i≤M}.\widetilde{D}=\operatorname{span}\{\widetilde{c}_{i}-\widetilde{c}_{1}:1\leq i\leq M\}.

By the sufficient-statistic construction above, the augmented experiment is equivalent to a Gaussian shift experiment on D~\widetilde{D}. All c~i\widetilde{c}_{i} have the same orthogonal projection ww onto D~⟂\widetilde{D}^{\perp}. Write

c~i=w+vi,vi∈D~.\widetilde{c}_{i}=w+v_{i},\qquad v_{i}\in\widetilde{D}. (94)

The sufficient statistics have means viv_{i}; the common component ww does not appear. Since w⟂D~w\perp\widetilde{D} and the c~i\widetilde{c}_{i} have equal norm,

∥vi∥2=E−∥w∥2=:r2\lVert v_{i}\rVert^{2}=E-\lVert w\rVert^{2}=:r^{2} (95)

is independent of ii, with 0≤r≤E0\leq r\leq\sqrt{E}, and dimD~≤M−1\dim\widetilde{D}\leq M-1.

If r>0r>0, divide the observation by N0/2\sqrt{N_{0}/2} and apply Corollary 2.5 together with the maximum-likelihood identity to the unit vectors vi/rv_{i}/r, after identifying D~\widetilde{D} with a Euclidean space and embedding it in ℝM−1\mathbb{R}^{M-1} if necessary. Their probability of correct decoding is no larger than that of a regular (M−1)(M-1)-simplex of radius rr. If r=0r=0, all finite-dimensional means coincide and the optimal probability is 1/M1/M.

We now compare different radii. Let 0≤r1≤r20\leq r_{1}\leq r_{2}, put σ2=N0/2\sigma^{2}=N_{0}/2, and consider a fixed regular simplex x1,…,xMx_{1},\ldots,x_{M}. If r2>0r_{2}>0, set η=r1/r2\eta=r_{1}/r_{2}. From the observation Y2=r2​xI+σ​ZY_{2}=r_{2}x_{I}+\sigma Z, form

K⁡(Y2)=η​Y2+σ​1−η2​Z′,K(Y_{2})=\eta Y_{2}+\sigma\sqrt{1-\eta^{2}}\,Z^{\prime}, (96)

where Z′Z^{\prime} is an independent standard Gaussian vector. Conditional on II, K⁡(Y2)K(Y_{2}) has the same law as r1​xI+σ​Z′′r_{1}x_{I}+\sigma Z^{\prime\prime}. Thus the radius-r1r_{1} experiment is a message-independent randomized degradation of the radius-r2r_{2} experiment. Composing a decoder for the former with this kernel may produce a randomized decoder for the latter. Randomization cannot improve Bayes success for finitely many hypotheses under zero–one loss: conditional on an observation, success is a linear function of the decision probabilities and is maximized by a deterministic maximum-a-posteriori rule. The optimal probability is therefore nondecreasing in rr. Equivalently, the smaller-radius experiment is a Blackwell degradation of the larger-radius experiment [6]. A regular simplex of radius E\sqrt{E} is feasible and attains the resulting upper bound. ∎

The equalization step uses the maximal energy constraint on each codeword. It does not yield the same conclusion under an average-over-codebook energy constraint.

E.3 Evaluation of the simplex decoding probability

Let e1,…,eMe_{1},\ldots,e_{M} be the standard basis of ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M} and set

A=E​MM−1,ui=A​ei,u¯=1M​∑j=1Muj.A=\sqrt{\frac{EM}{M-1}},\qquad u_{i}=Ae_{i},\qquad\bar{u}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}u_{j}. (97)

The centered vectors ui−u¯u_{i}-\bar{u} form a feasible regular simplex and

∥ui−u¯∥2=A2​(1−1M)=E.\lVert u_{i}-\bar{u}\rVert^{2}=A^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)=E. (98)

The orthogonal representatives uiu_{i} have squared norm E​M/(M−1)>EEM/(M-1)>E when M>1M>1 and are not asserted to be feasible codewords. They are used only to evaluate the equivalent translated experiment: adding the common vector u¯\bar{u} to every signal and to the observation is a deterministic bijection and leaves all likelihood ratios and optimal decoding probabilities unchanged.

Suppose message 11 is sent and write σ=N0/2\sigma=\sqrt{N_{0}/2}. In the orthogonal representation, correct maximum-likelihood decoding occurs when

A+σ​W1≥σ​Wj(2≤j≤M),A+\sigma W_{1}\geq\sigma W_{j}\qquad(2\leq j\leq M),

for independent standard Gaussian random variables W1,…,WMW_{1},\ldots,W_{M}. Conditioning on W1=WW_{1}=W gives

Pc∗​(E,M)=𝔼​Φ​(W+Aσ)M−1=pM​(2​E​M(M−1)​N0).P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M)=\mathbb{E}\Phi\!\left(W+\frac{A}{\sigma}\right)^{M-1}=p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right). (99)

By symmetry this is also the average success probability, proving (19).

The function pMp_{M} from (18) is continuous and

pM′​(a)=(M−1)​𝔼​[Φ​(W+a)M−2​φ​(W+a)]>0.p_{M}^{\prime}(a)=(M-1)\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Phi(W+a)^{M-2}\varphi(W+a)\right]>0. (100)

At a=0a=0, the random variable Φ⁡(W)\Phi(W) is uniform on (0,1)(0,1), so pM​(0)=1/Mp_{M}(0)=1/M. Dominated convergence gives pM​(a)↑1p_{M}(a)\uparrow 1 as a→∞a\to\infty. These facts prove the assertions about aM,ϵa_{M,\epsilon} and E∗​(M,ϵ)E^{*}(M,\epsilon) in Corollary 2.8. They also show that the set in (20) has a largest element. For fixed EE, the shift 2​E​M/((M−1)​N0)\sqrt{2EM/((M-1)N_{0})} remains bounded as M→∞M\to\infty, whereas the maximum of M−1M-1 independent standard Gaussian random variables diverges in probability. Therefore the correct-decoding probability tends to zero.
